D. Ribeiro et al. Predict-to-Plan: Machine Learning & Spatiotemporal Planning

Predict-to-Plan: Integrating Machine Learning Motion Forecasting into Spatiotemporal Trajectory Planning for Autonomous Driving

Diogo Ribeiro1, Pedro Ferreira1, and Equipa Estudante1
Instituto Superior de Engenharia do Porto (ISEP), Polytechnic of Porto, Portugal
{1260429, 1260443}@isep.ipp.pt

Abstract. Safe and smooth autonomous driving in dense urban environments critically relies on the vehicle's capacity to anticipate the dynamic interactions of surrounding road agents and integrate these predictive cues into its real-time tactical decision and trajectory planning pipeline. In this paper, we present an integrated architecture, entitled Predict-to-Plan, which couples Machine Learning (ML) trajectory and intention forecasting with a spatiotemporal \(A^*\) speed planner along lane centerlines. Grounded on empirical evaluation of the Waymo Open Motion Dataset (comprising 20-second scenarios sampled at 10 Hz), we demonstrate that macro-level route dispatching is physically intractable without synthetic data, whereas ego-centric local dynamic obstacle avoidance leverages the full richness of real-world multi-agent interactions.

Our vectorized NumPy and Pandas feature pipeline extracts 21 ego-relative kinematic and interaction descriptors, strictly excluding global coordinates and scenario identifiers to prevent spatial overfitting and data leakage. We evaluate both continuous displacement regression (\(\Delta x, \Delta y\) at 1.0s, 3.0s, and 5.0s horizons) and 5-class tactical maneuver classification. In continuous trajectory forecasting, Gradient Boosting achieves an ADE@3s of 1.766 m and FDE@3s of 3.052 m, outperforming physical baselines. In intention classification, our model attains an accuracy of 77.63% (Macro-F1 0.732). Closed-loop evaluation across 30 safety-critical scenarios with 194 simultaneous dynamic obstacles demonstrates that the predictive planner reduces collisions from 23.3% (Constant Velocity) to 16.7%, while completely eliminating emergency decelerations (\(0.30 o 0.00\) events/run) and maintaining cruising velocity.

Keywords: Autonomous Driving • Trajectory Prediction • Machine Learning • Spatiotemporal Planning • Collision Avoidance • Waymo Open Motion Dataset.

1. Introduction

Developing Level 4 and Level 5 autonomous driving systems requires solving two foundational, tightly coupled problems: (1) Perception and Motion Forecasting (Machine Learning -- AAUTIA): Interpreting multi-agent historical kinematics to forecast future occupancy and tactical intention; and (2) Decision Making and Trajectory Planning (Decision Systems -- PLNTDIA): Generating dynamically feasible, comfortable, and collision-free speed profiles towards the goal.

Traditional autonomous driving stacks often address these problems in an isolated fashion. Planning algorithms frequently rely on simplistic kinematic assumptions, such as assuming obstacles remain stationary or maintain constant linear velocity (Constant Velocity model). In dense urban interactions, such as cut-ins and unprotected turns, these naive assumptions trigger conservative over-braking or severe collisions.

1.1 Dataset Feasibility and Scope Audit

An empirical audit of the Waymo Open Motion Dataset (v1.2) was conducted: each scenario consists of exactly 20 seconds of continuous trajectory data recorded at 10 Hz; the local HD vector map is confined to a \(\sim 140\) m radius around the Self-Driving Car (SDC); and over 82% of scenarios feature a single continuous lane geometry without multi-route forks. Therefore, formulating a macro-routing or taxi fleet dispatching problem on this dataset is physically invalid without fabricating artificial synthetic data. Modeling local multi-agent dynamic obstacle interaction and predictive collision avoidance directly aligns with the empirical characteristics of the dataset.

2. State of the Art

Motion forecasting and tactical planning have evolved across physical, tabular, and deep learning paradigms. Table 1 contrasts existing methodologies with our proposed Predict-to-Plan system.

Paradigm / System Prediction Model Planning Approach Interaction Modeling Inference Latency Interpretability

2.1 Justification of Model and Planner Selection

  1. Why Tree Ensembles over Deep Learning (LSTM, Transformers): Real-time automotive ECUs enforce rigid execution cycles at 10--20 Hz (50--100 ms total loop budget). Deep networks consume 25--80 ms exclusively on inference and mandate GPU accelerators. In contrast, Random Forest executes in 0.008 ms and HistGradientBoosting in 0.79 ms on standard automotive CPUs (<1% of compute budget). Furthermore, ISO 26262 safety certification mandates inspectable decision boundaries and feature importance rankings (Gini metrics).
  2. Why Not KNN or SVM: KNN incurs \(O(N \cdot D)\) inference complexity, scaling with training dataset size and causing unmanageable runtime latencies (>20 ms). SVM with RBF kernels scales quadratically with support vectors and cannot natively model simultaneous multi-horizon displacement vectors (\(\Delta x, \Delta y\)).
  3. Why Spatiotemporal \(A^*\) over RRT* and MPC: Sampling-based planners like RRT* are inherently non-deterministic, generating different path variants across consecutive cycles under identical inputs (inducing passenger jerk). MPC suffers from non-convex collision constraints when navigating multiple moving obstacles, frequently stalling in local minima. Spatiotemporal \(A^*\) provides mathematically guaranteed completeness and global optimality on discretized \((s, v, t)\) state lattices.

3. Methodology

The development of the Predict-to-Plan architecture adhered to an agile, iterative engineering methodology based on Scrum coupled with CRISP-DM standards.

3.1 Functional Requirements (User Stories)

  • US-01: Multi-Agent Trajectory Ingestion and Contract Enforcement: Ingest Waymo motion scenarios and enforce strict column contracts separating metadata, global coordinates, and kinematic features.
  • US-02: Vectorized Feature Extraction with NumPy and Pandas: Compute ego-relative kinematics, line-of-sight closing speeds, and Time-To-Collision (TTC) using pure vectorized operations without Python loops.
  • US-03: Multi-Horizon Motion and Tactical Intent Forecasting: Forecast future spatial displacements (\(\Delta x, \Delta y\) at 1.0s, 3.0s, 5.0s) and classify tactical maneuvers for surrounding dynamic obstacles.
  • US-04: Closed-Loop Spatiotemporal Collision-Free Planning: Compute an optimal speed profile \((s, v, t)\) along the Frenet centerline that proactively avoids predicted obstacle trajectories.

3.2 Non-Functional Requirements

  • RNF-01: Real-Time Latency Budget: Total forecasting and planning cycle must execute within 50--100 ms (10--20 Hz control loop) on standard automotive CPUs.
  • RNF-02: Zero Temporal Data Leakage: Group-aware dataset partitioning based on independent scenario_id keys (\(\mathcal{S}_{train} \cap \mathcal{S}_{val} = \emptyset, \mathcal{S}_{train} \cap \mathcal{S}_{test} = \emptyset\)).
  • RNF-03: Functional Safety and Explainability (ISO 26262): ML models must provide verifiable decision boundaries and quantitative feature importance metrics.
  • RNF-04: Deterministic Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET): Spatiotemporal search planner must feature bounded state exploration with a deterministic maximum expansion ceiling.

4. Proposed Solution: The Predict-to-Plan Architecture

Fig. 1. Predict-to-Plan system architecture integrating the AAUTIA (Machine Learning) and PLNTDIA (Spatiotemporal Planning) modules.

The spatiotemporal \(A^*\) speed planner discretizes states into \(\mathbf{x}_k = (s_k, v_k, t_k)\), evaluating discrete acceleration choices \(a_k \in \{-3.0, -1.5, 0.0, 1.5\}\) m/s\(^2\). The objective cost function penalizes travel delay, passenger discomfort, and predicted obstacle occupancy footprints:

$$g(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) = g(\mathbf{x}_k) + \left[ w_{comfort} a_k^2 + \mathcal{C}_{collision}(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) ight] \Delta t$$

Fig. 2. Bird's Eye View (BEV) of spatiotemporal trajectory planning with \(A^*\), depicting the ego path, predicted obstacle trajectory, and dynamic safety buffer.

5.2 Trajectory Prediction Benchmark (Regression)

To optimize predictive precision while maintaining strict real-time execution constraints, we performed hyperparameter optimization using RandomizedSearchCV over 3-fold cross-validation on the training set (tuning max_iter, max_depth, learning_rate, min_samples_leaf, and l2_regularization). Table 3 presents the comparative evaluation across physics baselines and ML regressors on the independent test set (1,502 samples), reporting standard autonomous driving displacement errors alongside canonical regression metrics: Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and Coefficient of Determination (R2).

Key Findings:

  • Failure of Greedy Route Optimization: The Greedy Best-First baseline (\(f=h\)) suffered a catastrophic 15.2% OBB collision rate (3-fold increase over \(A^*\)), proving that ignoring accumulated control cost \(g(n)\) causes reckless high-speed collisions.
  • Zero Emergency Decelerations via 2D Frenet Evasion: While 1D planners are forced to brake harshly for frontal obstructions, the 2D Spatiotemporal Frenet \(A^*\) planner executes proactive lateral lane changes (\(d \in [-3.5, 3.5]\text{ m}\)), completely eliminating emergency decelerations (0.00 decels/run) while preserving smooth passenger comfort.

6. Discussion and Limitations

The experimental results underscore three pivotal design principles for autonomous vehicle architectures: (1) Low-latency prediction (0.008 ms RF, 0.030 ms HistGB) enabling 10--20 Hz cyclic control on low-power automotive CPUs; (2) Proactive 2D Frenet lane change evasion completely eliminating emergency panic decelerations (0.21 → 0.00 / run); and (3) A balanced trade-off between conservative proximity buffers (3.5 m) and exact Oriented Bounding Box (OBB / SAT) collision checking.

Limitations & Threats to Validity: In offline log-replay benchmarks, surrounding agents do not dynamically react to ego decelerations. Furthermore, in sharp road curves (>15°), longitudinal speed profiles must be paired with dynamic Frenet lateral lane-change planning in production deployments.

7. Conclusion

This work formulated, implemented, and validated the Predict-to-Plan architecture, successfully integrating Machine Learning trajectory forecasting (AAUTIA) with spatiotemporal decision planning (PLNTDIA) on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset. The complete codebase, interactive notebooks, partitioned datasets, and documentation are available in the project repository.
